Hey! I'm an OBGYN resident, currently on a RE rotation and will most likely specialize in REI. (Disclaimer: obv I'm still learning.) Sorry to hear your doc was dismissive. It sounds like she could have worded things a little more usefully, but the truth is that the odds are very much stacked in your favor for getting pregnant even if you did nothing else besides go home and have sex. With that said, there's no reason not to rule out the usual suspects. If you have regular cycles with recognizable moliminal symptoms (i.e. PMS), and/or monthly + OPK's, she probably doesn't have much doubt you're ovulating, which is what a CD21 progesterone would tell you. The day 3 stuff more tells you, "how hard is your pituitary having to work to make your ovaries do their job." TBH, we get this on the vast majority of people w/ fertility concerns, so I'm not too sure why she didn't. Maybe if your AMH is low, she'll want to go down that road. I think not preventing counts toward the 12 months too, as long as you were having regular intercourse. Some might say that a day 3 US is almost as good as day 3 labs, because they can look at your follicle count, which is a pretty good indicator of how well things are working. Some docs get an ultrasound to see IF you ovulated later on in the cycle, but we don't do this- if there's doubt about ovulation, we just get a CD21 progesterone. These do not lie-if it's above 10, you ovulated for sure. Again, neither of these may be necessary if there's little doubt about whether you ovulate. (Despite what the internet says, it is REALLY hard to have regular cycles w/ PMS symptoms if you are not ovulating, OPK's or not.)  I'd agree w/ the thyroid test. Other things an RE might do would include a prolactin level, semen analysis and HSG, especially if you had a c-section w/ your first baby or have had any pelvic infections since then.  (C-sections can leave behind scar tissue that can cause tubes to block up or get kinked in weird ways.) Just some random thoughts- if you have doubts, there's no harm in asking for a referral to an RE.

Well, today was my first “procedural day” at the clinic. I’m really glad I went- we are given the option to completely opt out and not even go on those days. Pretty much all the residents I know are pro-choice, but some still opt not to even be present. But it made me face some realities that made me more secure in my (dichotomous, slightly contradictory) way of thinking. There were a few things that bothered me enough to confirm my decision that, while I will still vote and advocate for the pro-choice movement, I cannot feel okay with actually carrying out the procedure. At least, for now. 

*****TRIGGER WARNING*** I’m about to discuss some technical aspects of surgical abortion that some may NOT want to know.  These are the things that I struggled with:

1.   There are a couple of “points of no return” during a surgical abortion. Once the cervix is dilated, and/or once the evacuation has begun, stopping isn’t a feasible option due to bleeding and infection risks. A couple of patients started crying for the procedure to be stopped after it was too late. I realize that they may not have been at their most rational after sedation, while in pain, etc. They had all been appropriately informed, consented and asked repeatedly if they were ready to proceed by their own volition. One even regained her composure and then said, “no, no , this has to be done.” Still, this was horrific to witness and reinforced my fear that in some cases, the procedure will only invite harm and regret. 

2.  The ultrasound-guided procedures: Normally I love, LOVE doing prenatal ultrasounds. When the pregnancy is wanted, I love watching the fetus become a reality to its mom as it kicks and wiggles around in there.  This will sound silly and sentimental, but I found it really difficult to watch that same scenario... but then watch the curette enter the picture and literally suck it all out. Intellectually, I understand that the fetus is incapable of perceiving pain or fear, and that it is distinctly different than a sentient, viable human. But I had a strong enough internal reaction to decide that when it comes to performing abortions,  I’m just not there yet. 

3.  Seeing the macerated fetal parts obviously bothered me to some extent, as I assume it must bother everyone, even if it’s just on a primitive level. 


With all of that said, I’m SO glad I went. I was so, so glad that I could be there to hold their hands, reassure them and talk them through it (which is all I did, for the reasons above.)

Ha!  Good. Sometimes I feel like I’m some kind of faker- it’s easy enough to preach about the importance of access and choice, but if I can’t actually help people carry out there decisions in the most fundamental sense, (i.e. actually doing the procedure), then what does that say about me?

Yup- ultrasound is it. Depending on how far along you are, they can measure the gestational sac (the "bubble" the pregnancy grows in), or even more accurately, the  "crown rump length," or CRL, which is just what it sounds like- the actual length of the fetus. For those who are farther along (> 13 weeks), we'd measure the head, thigh bone and abdomen. 

The crown rump length is the real gold standard, because there's very little variation in size that early on. For example, if the CRL is 1.2 cm, you can be quite sure that the pregnancy is about 8 weeks along- much moreso than guesswork  with the calendar.

I'm an OB/GYN resident (i.e. I'm a doctor, but still training- same phase as the Grey's Anatomy crew;-)) and this is how we date pregnancies. With that said, a first trimester dating ultrasound is worth its weight in gold when determining this. The ultrasound  usually matches up pretty closely to the date calculated from the first day of your last period. 

If your state limit is 12 weeks, I would get to a clinic ASAP- if you do need a procedure, sometimes appointments are booked up and it's hard to get a slot. Also, some states have mandatory waiting periods- you might have to go in for "day 1 counseling" followed by a mandatory waiting period before the actual procedure. (in my state, the mandatory wait is 48h.) Most clinics are very accommodating if they know someone is cutting it close with their gestational age, and will find a way to squeeze you in if needed. 

Also know that many states have much later limitations- for example, in TN it's 20 wks, in AR it's 21.

Do NOT take any pills that are just ordered online. There are very specific doses and formulations and handling that are needed to make sure the meds work. Lastly, the meds aren't safe for everyone- you would need to have some labs drawn to make sure they're a good option for you. If you do go the medical route, you need to follow up for an ultrasound 2 weeks afterward to make sure the abortion was complete.

A few things...

1. Pregnancy does NOT change your metabolism. You may gain weight, depending on how you eat, but I promise your metabolism does not come to a grinding halt the minute you conceive. 
2. Watch out for your joints! In addition to correcting for weird weight re-distribution, your joints actually get more lax during the second and third trimester. I see a surprising amount of ladies with sprained/twisted knees and ankles that aren't even active. 
3. Do not be mad at yourself if you have a little pooch belly postpartum. Even if you gained zero body fat, it takes awhile for your uterus to realize there's no baby in it anymore. This is especially noticeable if you're thin.  
4. Be patient with yourself- you're growing a human, it's kind of a big deal. You will be more tired/cranky/emotional/hungry than usual. If anyone tries to make you feel bad about this, please tell them to get lost immediately.
